social_history.living_situation: Lives in college dormitory with roommate

patient.chief_complaint: Bizarre behavior, paranoia, and social withdrawal for one week
patient.history_present_illness: A 22-year-old right-handed woman with a history of generalized anxiety disorder was brought to the emergency department by her parents and college roommate after approximately one week of increasingly abnormal behavior. Per her roommate, the patient had been isolating herself in her room, refusing to attend classes, and had become increasingly suspicious that her friends were 'watching her' and 'talking about her behind her back.' She began barricading her door at night. Her parents noted she had stopped returning phone calls for five days, which was very unusual for her. When her mother finally reached her, she was speaking in a disorganized, tangential manner and accused her mother of being 'an imposter.' The patient herself reports feeling 'weird' and describes difficulty sleeping for about ten days, with nights where she does not sleep at all despite feeling exhausted. She has had no witnessed seizures and denies any focal neurological symptoms. She denies visual or auditory hallucinations but appears internally preoccupied at times during the interview. She did have a mild upper respiratory illness with low-grade fever approximately three weeks prior, which resolved spontaneously. Her friends noted she was 'completely normal' before this started. She has no prior psychiatric history and her anxiety has been well-controlled on sertraline for two years. There is no prior psychotic illness in the family. Vitals on arrival were notable for mild tachycardia.

differential.key_features: Age, acute behavioral change, paranoia, disorganized speech — but no prior psychiatric history, short prodrome, mild hyponatremia, tachycardia, and sleeping disturbance argue against primary psychiatric disorder
Viral prodrome 3 weeks prior, behavioral change — but HSV PCR negative, no temporal lobe signal on MRI, no fever, afebrile on presentation
Young woman, encephalopathy — but anti-TPO negative and TSH normal
College student — but urine drug screen negative, denied substance use, confirmed by roommate

optimal_actions.action: Order brain MRI with and without gadolinium
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal or near-normal MRI; does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture and send CSF for routine studies, HSV PCR, and anti-NMDAR antibodies
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Near-normal or mildly abnormal CSF; anti-NMDAR antibody result pending
Mild diffuse slowing; no extreme delta brush early in disease

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive metabolic labs including thyroid function, anti-TPO, toxicology screen
Send serum and CSF anti-NMDAR antibody panel to reference laboratory
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive anti-NMDAR IgG in serum and CSF

optimal_actions.action: Order pelvic ultrasound to rule out ovarian teratoma
Initiate first-line immunotherapy: IV methylprednisolone 1g/day x5 days + IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x5 days
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Begin immunotherapy to reduce antibody burden and CNS inflammation

optimal_actions.action: Urgent gynecology referral for surgical teratoma resection
Order extended autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Other antibodies negative, confirming NMDAR specificity

optimal_actions.action: Continuous cardiac monitoring and electrolyte correction

critical_actions: Perform lumbar puncture and send anti-NMDAR antibody panel — do not delay empirical immunotherapy if high suspicion
Order pelvic imaging (ultrasound) to identify ovarian teratoma — tumor removal is key to recovery
Do NOT rely on MRI to exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis — 50% of cases have normal MRI
Do NOT treat as primary psychiatric disorder with antipsychotics alone without investigating organic cause
Initiate empirical immunotherapy (steroids + IVIG) while awaiting antibody confirmatory results if clinical suspicion high
contraindicated_actions: Discharging with psychiatric referral only without CNS workup — this patient needs LP and MRI
Initiating long-term antipsychotic therapy as primary diagnosis without organic workup
Delaying LP due to normal CT scan — LP is essential for anti-NMDAR antibody testing
Attributing hyponatremia solely to poor oral intake without considering SIADH from CNS cause
key_reasoning_points: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis often presents initially as a psychiatric disorder (paranoia, agitation, insomnia) without seizures or obvious neurological signs, making early diagnosis challenging — this is the 'psychiatric prodrome'
A normal EEG and normal MRI do NOT exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis at this early stage; up to 50% of cases have a normal brain MRI
The temporal relationship between the viral prodrome 3 weeks prior and acute behavioral change is typical for autoimmune encephalitis
Mild hyponatremia in a young woman with new psychiatric symptoms should prompt consideration of CNS pathology causing SIADH
Anti-NMDAR antibody testing (serum AND CSF) is mandatory; CSF testing has higher specificity
Ovarian teratoma is found in ~58% of women with anti-NMDAR encephalitis; pelvic imaging is essential
First-line treatment: IV corticosteroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis; second-line: rituximab or cyclophosphamide for refractory cases
The clinical red herring here is the prior anxiety disorder diagnosis and the psychiatric presentation — the key is recognizing the acute, new-onset nature in someone without prior psychosis

red_herrings.data_point: Known history of generalized anxiety disorder on sertraline
red_herrings.intended_effect: Leads clinician to attribute behavioral changes to exacerbation of pre-existing anxiety/psychiatric disorder
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Pre-existing anxiety disorder is well-controlled and does not typically cause paranoia, insomnia, or disorganized speech; new-onset psychosis in a previously well-controlled anxiety patient requires organic workup

red_herrings.intended_effect: Leads clinician to exclude autoimmune or infectious encephalitis based on normal imaging
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Up to 50% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases have normal MRI; a normal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis

red_herrings.intended_effect: Leads clinician to conclude no CNS inflammation and discharge with psychiatric referral
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Early in the disease, CSF may be essentially normal; pleocytosis develops over days-weeks; anti-NMDAR antibody results are not yet available at time of initial LP

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: 22-year-old woman with psychiatric prodrome only — no seizures, normal MRI, near-normal CSF. Classic diagnostic puzzle presentation of anti-NMDAR encephalitis masquerading as first-break psychosis.
